cases.doc:
`post` was given a price at or below zero. Not a judgement about the value: a price
that is not positive is not a price, and the pool would refuse it anyway (E-003 \xc2\xa73.2).
Refusing here keeps it out of storage, where it would sit as the newest reading and
block every later post of the same second.
cases.name: BadPrice

cases.doc:
`post` was given a timestamp older than the stored one. The adapter holds the newest
publication, and accepting an older time would let a keeper that is looping on a cached
read overwrite a fresher price with a staler one. An equal timestamp is not this error
since the amendment of 2026-09-16 (spec \xc2\xa73.3): a corrected price under an unchanged
publication time is something the issuer said, and only the keeper can tell whether it
is worth posting.
cases.name: NotNewer

cases.doc: `post` was given a timestamp later than the ledger's. A publication time in the future\nis not a publication time; it would also poison the entry, because no honest later\nreading could then be newer.
cases.name: FromTheFuture

cases.doc: The constructor was given more than 18 decimals, which the pool refuses (E-003 \xc2\xa73.2),\nso the adapter could only ever be a source the pool skips.
cases.name: BadDecimals

function_v0.doc:
The keeper's one entry point: store what it read at the issuer (spec \xc2\xa73.3).

`timestamp` is the issuer's own publication time in seconds -- for Ondo the block time
of the Ethereum read, for Etherfuse `current_time` of the response, for Centrifuge the
block time of the event -- never the moment the keeper read and never the NAV's
valuation time. This contract cannot check which of the three it was given; nothing on
chain can. The keeper's readers carry that rule and its tests hold them to it (spec
\xc2\xa73.4, \xc2\xa74 test 5).

It refuses three things and three only. A price at or below zero is not a price. A
timestamp older than the stored one would let a keeper looping on a cached read
overwrite a fresher price with an older one. A timestamp later than the ledger's is not
a publication time, and would poison the entry, because no honest later reading could
then be newer.

function_v0.doc:
Rotation of the operational key (spec \xc2\xa73.3, ADR-007 point 5).

The keeper's key sits on an unattended machine, so this is the one transaction that
ends an incident with it: after it the old key can do nothing at all, because `post` is
the only thing a keeper could ever do and it is checked against the stored address on
every call. It does not touch `Latest`: a price the old keeper posted stays, and
whether it is still to be trusted is a matter for the guardian and the engine's gates,
not for a key rotation.

Errors: none of its own; a caller who is not governance fails on the authorisation.

function_v0.doc:
Fixes the two roles and the scale (spec \xc2\xa73.3).

`decimals` above [`DECIMALS_MAX`] is refused: the pool refuses more (E-003 \xc2\xa73.2), so
such an adapter could only ever be a source the pool skips. Every source of Rhumb is
deployed at 18 and the keeper scales every reading to 18 before posting (spec \xc2\xa73.4),
so that one number means the same thing at every source of every pool; a coarser scale
is accepted here because the pool accepts it, and is reported unchanged so that the
pool does the scaling.

`Latest` is not written: the adapter holds no price until the keeper posts one, and
`observe` answers `None` until then, which a pool reads as a source without an
observation (E-007 \xc2\xa73.2). A placeholder price would be a rate nobody published.
